Rule 62

The subjunctive mood is the verb form used for expressing a wish, a suggestion, a command, or a condition that is contrary to some fact. The form of a verb in the subjunctive mood may differ from the form with the same subject which is not in the subjunctive mood, like –

items.text: I was in your position two years ago. (not in the subjunctive mood)
If I were in your position, I would do the same. (subjunctive mood)
I wish it were still in use. (it was becomes it were)
She suggests that Anil work full time from Saturday. (Anil works becomes Anil work)
I suggest that he implement a budget cut in March. (he implements becomes he implement)

blocks.text: Rule 63

All the auxiliary verbs except be, do and have are called modals. Unlike other auxiliary verbs, modals only exist in their helping form; they cannot act alone as the main verbs in a sentence. Be, do and have also differ from the other auxiliaries in respect that they can also serve as ordinary verbs in a given sentence.
The modal verbs are: can / could / may / might / must / shall / should / ought to / will / would / dare / need / used to
Rule 64
Action verbs are verbs that show the performance of an action. They are dynamic verbs that show something happening. There are regular and irregular action verbs.

items.text: To walk is a regular action verb.
To run is an irregular action verb.

blocks.text: Rule 65
The third person singular (he/she/it/one) is the one which tends to be different from other conjugations. The regular verbs end in -s (or possibly -es).

items.text: He sees, She watches, It thinks, One does

blocks.text: Rule 66
The present participle is the root word + -ing. It's used in the past, present and future progressive tenses.

items.text: What are we doing today?
Ramesh is meeting with the professor after the class.
They've been living in Venezuela for three years.

blocks.text: Rule 67
The past and past participle for regular verbs is the root word + -ed. It's only used with the past tenses.

items.text: We shopped for hours on Saturday afternoon.
The books were stacked on the shelf.
He had played computer games for the whole weekend.

blocks.text: Rule 68
The simple past and past participle of irregular verbs can end in a variety of ways, with absolutely no consistent pattern.

items.text: to drive (infinitive) – drives (simple present) – drove (simple past) – driven (past participle) – driving (present participle)
to feel (infinitive) – feels (simple present) – felt (simple past) – felt (past participle) – feeling (present participle)
to swim (infinitive) – swims (simple present) – swam (simple past) – swum (past participle) – swimming (present participle)

blocks.text: Rule 69
A simple past tense verb always has just one part. You need no auxiliary verb to form this tense.

items.text: Despite the noise, jolts and jerks, John slept so soundly on the city bus that he missed his stop.
I saw a movie yesterday.
I didn't see a play yesterday.
Last year, I travelled to Japan.

blocks.text: Rule 70
When we state an event that shows something of the past time, Past Indefinite tense is used.

items.text: It rained heavily during our visit to the Taj last week.

blocks.text: Rule 71
We use Simple Present tense for the future when we refer to something that has been scheduled or arranged to happen at a particular time such as a timetable.

items.text: The first flight to Rome leaves at 6 a.m.
The special sales offer closes on August 31.
The public exhibition of a collection of his paintings ends in a week.

blocks.text: Rule 72
The simple future refers to a time later than now, and expresses facts or certainty. The simple future is used:

items.text: For predicting a future event: It will rain tomorrow.
With I or We, for expressing a spontaneous decision: I'll pay for the tickets by credit card.
For expressing willingness: He'll carry your bag for you.
In the negative form, for expressing unwillingness: The baby won't drink his soup.
With I in the interrogative form using 'shall', for making an offer: Shall I open the window?
With we in the interrogative form using 'shall', for making a suggestion: Shall we go to the cinema tonight?
With I in the interrogative form using 'shall', for asking for advice or instructions: What shall I tell the boss about this money?
With you, for giving orders : You will do exactly as I say.
With you in the interrogative form, for giving an invitation: Will you come to the dance with me?

blocks.text: Rule 73

Most sentences using the conditional contain the word 'if'. The zero conditional is often used for referring to general truths. The tense in both parts of the sentence is the simple present. In zero conditional sentences, the word 'if' can usually be replaced by the word 'when' without changing the meaning.

items.text: If this thing happens, that thing happens.
If you heat ice, it melts.

blocks.text: Rule 74

There are three type of conditional sentences :
(a) open condition sentence
(b) Improbable, Unlikely or Imaginary or Hypothetical condition
(c) Impossible/Closed condition

items.text: If one buys a car, it costs money.
If I know the answer, I will tell you.
If he worked hard, he would pass.
If I were in his place, I would wait a little longer.
If you had worked hard, you would have passed.
If I had known his address, I would have told you.

blocks.text: The first two examples belong to (a), the next two to (b), and the last two to (c).
Rule 75
Many multipart verbs, however, require the past participle after one or more auxiliary verbs.

items.text: Seema had bitten into the muffin before Parul mentioned that it was her infamous chocolate-vanilla variety. — Here, had = auxiliary verb; bitten = past participle
Once Prateek has written his essay for Raju, he plans to reward himself with a packet of chocolates. — Here, has = auxiliary verb; written = past participle
Rashmi might have slept better if she hadn't watched The Jurassic Park on Star Movies. — Here, might have = auxiliary verbs; slept = past participle

blocks.text: Rule 76
For regular verbs, knowing the distinction between the simple past and past participle is unnecessary because both are identical.

items.text: Sapna giggled as the clown rubbed his cold wet nose into the elephant's stomach. — Here, giggled = simple past

Until the disapproving Mrs. Kapoor elbowed Kavita in the ribs, the young girl had giggled without stop at the coloured sticker attached to her friend's collar. — Here, had = auxiliary verb; giggled = past participle

blocks.text: Check out these two sentences:
Rule 77
When you choose an irregular verb for a sentence, however, the simple past and past participle are often different. Hence, you must know the distinction.

items.text: Rajib drove so cautiously that traffic piled up behind him, causing angry drivers to honk their horns and shout. — Here, drove = simple past
Rajib might have driven faster if he hadn't forgotten his glasses and saw more than big coloured blurs through the windshield. — Here, might have = auxiliary verbs; driven = past participle

blocks.text: Read the following examples :
Rule 78
We use the modal verbs 'can', 'may', 'must' to express various meanings, like ability, possibility, permission, attitudes, opinions, etc.
Rule 79
The word 'return' can mean a number of things.

items.text: To give back / bring back – I returned the books yesterday.
To hit back – Federer returned Nadal's serves beautifully.
To go back – She returned from Australia last month.
To send back – The students returned the papers to the teacher.
To pay back – He returned all the money he had taken.

blocks.text: Remember that the use of 'return back' is wrong. The word 'back' should not be used after 'return'. It is superfluous (unnecessary).
Rule 80
The modal verb 'can' is used for describing the ability to do something.

items.text: I can swim very well.
Can he speak English fluently?
We cannot sing at all.

blocks.text: Rule 81
The modal verb 'can' expresses the possibility to do something.

items.text: We can go to the seaside at last. Our holidays start next week.

blocks.text: Rule 82
We use the modal verb 'can' to say that something is probable.

items.text: It can be John. He has blond hair and he is wearing glasses.

blocks.text: Rule 83
The modal verb 'can' expresses the permission to do something.

items.text: Why not? You can marry her. She is a nice girl.

blocks.text: Rule 84
The modal auxiliary verb 'may' is used for seeking permission.

items.text: You may borrow my car. I won't need it.
May I sit here?

blocks.text: Rule 85
The modal verb 'may' is used for expressing probability or prediction.

items.text: They may call you tomorrow.

blocks.text: Rule 86
The main difference between 'may' and 'can' is the style. 'May' is more formal than 'can'. The opposite of 'may' is 'must not' or 'may not'.

items.text: May I eat this chocolate?
You mustn't smoke here. (strong prohibition)

blocks.text: Rule 87
The modal auxiliary verb 'must' is used for a strong obligation. It is personal, because it shows the speaker's opinion or will.

items.text: I must clean my teeth. I want to be healthy.
You must go there. And do it right now.

blocks.text: Rule 88
The modal verb 'must' is used for expressing a strong recommendation.

items.text: You must see it. It's the best film I've ever seen.

blocks.text: Rule 89
We use 'must' to express the certainty of the speaker.

items.text: They must be at school by now. It's already 9 o'clock.

blocks.text: Rule 90
Note that the opposite of 'must' is 'don't have to' as both 'must' and 'have to' show obligation.

items.text: Mom, must I wash up? No, you don't have to. I've already done it.

blocks.text: Rule 91
You should remember that 'must not' has a different meaning. It is used for expressing prohibition that involves the speaker's will.

items.text: We mustn't come late today. Or the teacher will be very angry.
He mustn't enter this room. It is dangerous.

blocks.text: Rule 92
With both a singular and a plural subject dare not or daren't is used in a negative sentence.

items.text: I daren't (dare not) challenge her.
She dare not oppose me.

blocks.text: Rule 93

A double negative is usually produced by combining the negative form of verb (e.g., cannot, did not, have not) with a negative pronoun (e.g., nothing, nobody), a negative adverb (e.g., never, hardly) or a negative conjunction (e.g., neither/nor).

items.text: I didn't see nothing.
I did not have neither her address nor her phone number.
It wasn't uninteresting.
She is not unattractive.
He didn't see nothing.  =  He saw something.
She claims she has not seen neither Paul nor John.  =  She claims she has seen either Paul or John.

blocks.text: Remember that a double negative gives the sentence a positive sense.
Rule 94
In present tense, regular verbs use the root form, except for the third person singular (which ends in -s).

items.text: First person singular: I write
Second person singular: You write
Third person singular: He/She/It writes
First person plural: We write
Second person plural: You write
Third person plural: They write

blocks.text: Rule 95
Irregular present tense verbs are things like to be, which change form for each person.

items.text: First person singular: I am
Second person singular: You are
Third person singular: He/She/It is
First person plural: We are
Second person plural: You are
Third person plural: They are

blocks.text: Rule 96
When there are two subjects in a sentence and they are not in the same number, we must use a separate auxiliary (am, is, are, was, were, has, have) for each of them.

items.text: Three were killed and one was injured.
It is wrong to say – Three killed and one were injured.

blocks.text: Rule 97
A single verb should be made to serve two subjects only when the form of the verb is the same for both the subjects.

items.text: I am seventeen years old and my sister is fourteen.
It is wrong to say – I am seventeen years old and my sister fourteen.

blocks.text: Rule 98
Two auxiliaries can be used with one principal verb only when the form of the principal verb is appropriate to both the auxiliaries.

items.text: He never has taken, and never will take such strong measures.
It is wrong to say – He never has, and never will take such strong measures.

blocks.text: Rule 99
When there is only one auxiliary and two principal verbs, it should be correctly associated with the both.

items.text: Ten candidates have passed, one has failed.
It is wrong to say – Ten candidates have passed, one failed.

blocks.text: Rule 100
When the subordinate clause comes after 'lest', the auxiliary verb 'should' must be used, whatever be the tense of the verb in the main clause.

items.text: We start early lest we should miss the train.
It is wrong to say – We start early lest we shall miss the train.

blocks.text: Rule 101
We use 'be used to + verb-ing' to talk about things which feel normal for us or things that we are accustomed to.

items.text: I'm used to getting up early, so I don't mind doing it (= getting up early is normal for me, it's what I usually do).

blocks.text: Rule 102
While using 'used to', we make the negative or the question with the verb 'be' in the normal way. The 'used to' doesn't change.

items.text: Ajay isn't used to staying up late, so he's very tired today.
Are your children used to walking a lot?

blocks.text: Rule 103
We can also use 'be used to + noun', which has the same meaning.

items.text: I've lived in Cherrapunji almost all my life, so I'm used to rain (= rain is normal for me).
That football team always lose, so they're used to disappointment.

blocks.text: Rule 104
We can put the verb 'be' into any tense. So we can talk about things in the past or the future as well as the present using this expression.

items.text: It was difficult when I first started university, because I wasn't used to the amount of work we had to do.
Soon I'll be used to driving in Delhi and I won't be so frightened.

blocks.text: Rule 105
We can use 'get used to + verb-ing' to talk about the change of not normal to normal. We can also use this in any tense.

items.text: Don't worry if your new job is hard at first. You'll get used to it.
It took me a while, but I got used to speaking another language every day.

blocks.text: Rule 106
If a gerund is preceded by a pronoun, that pronoun must be in possessive case.

items.text: He emphasized my going there.
It is wrong to say – He emphasized me going there.

blocks.text: Rule 107

The Present Perfect Continuous tense is used for an action that began in the past time and still going at the time of speaking. It is used with adverbials of time introduced by 'since', 'for' and 'how long'.

items.text: How long have you been working in this office?
It is wrong to say – How long are you working in this office?

blocks.text: Rule 108

The present continuous of any verb is composed of two parts - the present tense of the verb to be + the present participle of the main verb. The form of the present participle is: base+ing, e.g. talking, playing, moving, smiling. The usage of 'have' in any continuous tense is forbidden.

items.text: I am going to school.
Birds are flying in the sky.

blocks.text: Rule 109
A verb when preceded by a preposition must be in the form of gerund.

items.text: They were punished for coming late.
It is wrong to say – They were punished for come late.

blocks.text: Rule 110
The Future Indefinite tense is not used in the clauses of time, place and condition. Here, the Present Indefinite tense is used.

items.text: I shall wait for you, till you finish your work.
It is wrong to say – I shall wait for you till you will finish your work.

blocks.text: Rule 111
The Present Perfect tense is not used with the adverbs of past time, like yesterday, in 2005, etc. Here, Past Indefinite tense is used.

items.text: I bought a cycle yesterday.
It is wrong to say – I have bought a cycle yesterday.

blocks.text: Rule 112

We use Present Perfect tense when we want to talk about unfinished actions that started in the past and continue to the present. Usually, we use it to say 'how long' an action or state has continued with 'since' and 'for'.

items.text: I have known Shravan since 1994.
She has lived in London for three years.

blocks.text: Rule 113
The Past Perfect tense is used for representing the earlier of the past two actions.

items.text: When I reached the station, the train had already left.

blocks.text: It is wrong to say – When I reached the station, the train already left.
Rule 114
In order to state something which resembles a general truth or habitual truth, Simple Present tense is used.

items.text: The sky is blue.
Birds fly in the sky.

blocks.text: Rule 115
Past tense in the main clause should be followed by Past tense in the subordinate clause.

items.text: He succeeded because he worked hard.

blocks.text: It is wrong to say – He succeeded because he works hard.
Rule 116
Past tense in the main clause may be followed by Present tense in the subordinate clause when the subordinate clause expresses a universal truth.

items.text: Our teacher said that the earth revolves around the sun.

blocks.text: It is wrong to say – Our teacher said that the earth revolved around the sun.
Rule 117
Modal auxiliaries are not used together. But two auxiliaries can be connected by a conjunction.

items.text: He should and must do it.

blocks.text: It is wrong to say – He should must do it.
Rule 118
When ‘need’ and ‘dare’ is followed by ‘not’, it turns into a modal auxiliary. In such situations, it takes bare-infinitive and we cannot use ‘needs not’ or ‘dares not’.

items.text: He need not do it.

blocks.text: It is wrong to say – He needs not do it.
Rule 119

We use the Present Continuous tense for definite future arrangements. Often, it doesn’t really matter if we choose ‘be going to’ or the present continuous. Look at the examples below where you will notice very little difference in their meanings.

items.text: I’m doing this work tonight.
I’m going to do this work tonight.

blocks.text: Rule 120
We use the Simple Present tense in two cases. First, we use it for a time-tabled event in the future, like public transport and secondly for the start of a class.

items.text: My train leaves at six tonight.
His class starts at 9am tomorrow.

blocks.text: Rule 121
We also use Simple Present tense after certain words, when the sentence has a future meaning. These words are: before / after / as soon as/ until / when.

items.text: I’ll call you when I get home.
She’s going to study after she finishes dinner.
Please drink some juice as soon as you complete the race.

blocks.text: Rule 122
Many verbs have a transitive and an intransitive form.

items.text: John ate the pizza (transitive).
John ate (intransitive).

blocks.text: Rule 123
Some verbs that have more than one meaning can be transitive or intransitive depending on which meaning is being used.

items.text: I see the mountains (see = see with your eyes, transitive).
I see (see = understand, intransitive).

blocks.text: Rule 124
A transitive verb must have a direct object.

items.text: I enjoyed the party.
Ravi likes chocolates.

blocks.text: It is wrong to say – I enjoyed. It is wrong to say – Ravi likes
Rule 125
An intransitive verb can’t have a direct object. Intransitive verbs also can’t make passive.

items.text: They arrived. — Here, the subject is ‘they’ and the verb is ‘arrived’. There’s no object.
The children are sleeping. — The subject is ‘the children’ and the verb is ‘are sleeping’. There’s no object.

blocks.text: Note : without an object in a sentence, passive is not possible.
Rule 126

There are some verbs which we call state, non-continuous or stative verbs. These verbs aren’t used in continuous tenses (like the present continuous, or the future continuous). These verbs often describe states that last for some time.

Some of the common stative verbs are: like, know, hate, want, prefer, believe, belong, agree, remember, smell, taste, sound, etc. A verb which isn’t stative is called a dynamic verb, and is usually an action.
Rule 127
Some verbs can be both stative and dynamic. ‘Be’ – is usually a stative verb, but when it is used in the continuous it means ‘behaving’ or ‘acting’.

items.text: You are stupid. = it’s part of your personality
You are being stupid. = only now, not usually
‘Think’ – (stative) = have an opinion
I think that coffee is great.
‘Think’ – (dynamic) = consider; have in my head
What are you thinking about? I’m thinking about my next holiday.
‘Have’ – (stative) = own
I have a car. ‘Have’ – (dynamic) = part of an expression
I’m having a party / a picnic / a bath / a good time / a break.
‘See’ – (stative) = see with your eyes / understand
I see what you mean. I see her now; she’s just coming along the road.
‘See’ – (dynamic) = meet / have a relationship with
I’ve been seeing my boyfriend for three years.
I’m seeing Mr. Kapoor tomorrow.
‘Taste’ – (stative) = has a certain taste
This soup tastes great.
The coffee tastes really bitter.
‘Taste’ – (dynamic) = the action of tasting
The chef is tasting the soup.

blocks.text: Rule 128
An adjective is a word or set of words that modifies (i.e. describes) a noun or pronoun. Adjectives may come before the words they modify.

items.text: That is a cute puppy.
She likes a high school senior.

blocks.text: Rule 129
Adjectives may also follow the words they modify.

items.text: That puppy looks cute.
The technology is state-of-the-art.

blocks.text: Rule 130
We use an adjective to describe the qualities of people, things, places etc.

items.text: She’s a young woman.
He’s a great singer.

blocks.text: Rule 131
We use adjectives after ‘linking’ verbs, such as be, become, feel, seem, smell, sound, look, taste, etc.

items.text: It looks interesting.
It tastes delicious.
His ideas are interesting.

blocks.text: Rule 132
Sometimes, the adjective follows a verb, but it describes a noun or pronoun that comes before the verb.

items.text: These strawberries taste sour.
The pickles are salty.

blocks.text: Rule 133
Adjectives are used either attributively or predicatively.

items.text: It is an easy problem. (attributively)
The problem is easy. (predicatively)

blocks.text: Rule 134
We can use an adjective to describe the object of a sentence.

items.text: His answer made his boss angry.

blocks.text: Rule 135
Adjectives tell us how much – or how many – of something we’re talking about.

items.text: Please use three white flowers in the arrangement. — Here, three and white are modifying flowers.

blocks.text: Rule 136
We use ‘no longer’ or ‘not any longer’ to talk about the end of an action or state. ‘No longer’ is more formal.

items.text: One day I could stand it no longer.
I couldn’t stand it any longer. I walked out and didn’t go back.
She no longer wears the dull colours of her former life and now dresses in bright, fashionable clothes.

blocks.text: ‘No longer’ often comes in the normal mid position for adverbs (between the subject and the main verb, or after the modal verb or first auxiliary verb, or after be as a main verb), especially in more formal styles.
Rule 137
‘Unlikely’ is an adjective; while ‘unlike’ is used as a preposition more often than not, although in formal contexts it can be used as an adjective with the meaning of dissimilar.

items.text: It is very unlikely that it will rain today.
I am unlike my sister in many ways.
Unlike most systems, this one is very easy to install.
The project seemed unlikely to succeed.

blocks.text: Unlikely means = improbable; not likely. Unlike means = dissimilar to; not alike; not like; different from
Rule 138
Cardinal adjectives are those types of numbers that answer the question, ‘how many?’

items.text: How many birds are there in the backyard?
There are zero birds.
There are no birds.
How many balls are on the court?
There is one ball. — Here, One = Cardinal number adjective; Ball = singular noun – representing one (1).
Tomorrow is our twelfth day of vacation.
This is the fourth time I’ve seen this movie.
This is the second time I’ve been the ninth best runner in this race.

blocks.text: Saying there are ‘no’ birds is the same as saying there are ‘zero’ birds. If you want to say there is one (1), this requires a singular noun. Ordinal adjectives are numbers used for showing order in a series. You should always use the article ‘the’ before an ordinal number. For all other Ordinal numbers use the Cardinal numbers + ‘th’, like the fourth – the 4th; the sixth – the 6th; the seventy-sixth – the 76th
Rule 139
The word ‘broadcast’ means to communicate or transmit (a signal, a message, or content, such as audio or video programming) – broadcast, broadcasting, broadcasts (verb).

items.text: I was watching television when the news was broadcast.
The concert will be broadcast live tomorrow evening.

blocks.text: Its five forms (participles) are: broadcast – broadcasts – broadcasting – broadcast – broadcast. It is wrong to say ‘broadcasted’.
Rule 140

A single adjective made up of two or more words is called a compound adjective. The words in a compound adjective can be linked together by a hyphen (or hyphens) to show they are part of the same adjective.

items.text: The security person has a heavy-metal detector.
I saw a green-eyed vulture.
He bought a four-room house.
The pilot flew a two-seater aircraft.

blocks.text: The easiest compound adjectives to spot are the ones that include numbers. Look at the structure : Numeral Adjective + Hyphen + Noun. If a compound word is formed by joining a Definite Numeral Adjective and a Noun by a hyphen, then that Noun is always singular.
Rule 141

Distributive adjectives are normally used with singular nouns. They include ‘each’, ‘every’, ‘either’ and ‘neither’ and are used for referring to the members of a group as individuals. After each of these distributive adjectives, a plural subject is used, while the verb remains singular.

items.text: Each participant was asked to complete a survey. (When the noun to which ‘each’ refers is plural, the construction ‘each of the’ is used.)

Every participant was asked to complete a survey. (It would never be appropriate to use ‘every of the’ – as in, ‘every of the participants’, which is wrong. ‘Every’ is only used with a singular noun.)
Either of these movies would be interesting to me. (‘Either’ implies one or the other of two options.)
Neither pen will do, as I need to sign in pencil. (‘Neither’ implies not one or the other of two options.)

blocks.text: Rule 142

Adjectives have many different endings. Many adjectives are created simply by adding certain suffixes to words that were previously nouns or verbs. Some adjectives end in ‘-ful’. These adjectives describe nouns or pronouns that are full of something or have a lot of something.

items.text: a joyful smile ; a useful book ; a beautiful face

blocks.text: Rule 143
Some adjectives end in ‘-ous’.

items.text: a poisonous snake ; a famous writer ; a dangerous job

blocks.text: Rule 144
Some adjectives end in ‘-y’.

items.text: dirty hands; a sunny day; stormy weather

blocks.text: Rule 145
Some adjectives end in ‘-less’. These adjectives describe a person or thing that does not have something.

items.text: a meaningless word; a cloudless sky; seedless grapes

blocks.text: Rule 146
Some adjectives end in ‘-al’.

items.text: actual, mental, physical, special

blocks.text: Rule 147
There are some adjectives that end in ‘-ic’, ‘-ish’, ‘-ible’, ‘-able’, ‘-ive’ and ‘-ly’.

items.text: a fantastic dancer, a selfish boy, visible footprints, comfortable place, expensive jewellery, friendly manner

blocks.text: Rule 148
Many adjectives end in ‘-ing’.

items.text: a smiling face, loving parents, a caring nurse

blocks.text: Rule 149
Many adjectives end in ‘-ed’.

items.text: satisfied customers, boiled eggs, wasted time

blocks.text: Rule 150
Many adjectives end in ‘-ar’.

items.text: familiar, regular, popular

blocks.text: Rule 151

Adjectives usually go before nouns (e.g. a small child) unless one of the following verbs is involved: be, feel, taste, smell, sound, look, appear, seem. In these cases, adjectives work more like adverbs.

items.text: The child is small ; The child seems small.

blocks.text: Rule 152
While contemplating the relationship between adjectives and verbs, you should always remember that adjectives can come after verbs.

items.text: The rock star was crazy ; The cat's tail is long.
That shirt looks great on you.

blocks.text: Rule 153

It is important to note that verbs that turn into adjectives are called participles. Usually, the verb has -ing at the end of the root form, or it's the past tense. The adjective can be placed before the noun or after the verb.

items.text: The smiling baby is really cute. — Here, smiling is used as an adjective, as is cute.
This is my new washing machine. — Here, washing is acting like an adjective for machine.

blocks.text: Rule 154
Many adjectives are participle forms of verbs. The '-ed' form describes how someone feels (bored). The '-ing' form describes the person or thing that causes the feeling (boring).

items.text: She was too frightened to say a word.
It was a boring film.

blocks.text: Rule 155
Possessive adjectives are used for showing possession or ownership of something. While we use them when we refer to people, it is more in the sense of relationship than ownership.
The possessive adjectives are: I – my, you – your, he – his, she – her, it – its, we – our, you – your, they – their
Rule 156
The possessive adjective needs to agree with the possessor and not with the thing that is possessed.

items.text: My car is very old; Our dog is black ; Their homework is on the table.

blocks.text: Rule 157

Like all adjectives, possessive adjectives are always located directly in front of the noun they refer to. (Possessive Adjective + Noun) We do not include an '-s' to the adjective when the noun is plural like in many other languages.

items.text: Our cars are expensive.
It is wrong to say – Ours cars are expensive. (Incorrect)

blocks.text: Rule 158
When there are two or more adjectives before a noun, opinion adjectives come before fact adjectives. Fact adjectives appear as follows: size - age - colour - origin - material

items.text: a silly old man ; It is wrong to say – an old silly man
a beautiful blue butterfly; It is wrong to say – a blue beautiful butterfly
a new red dress ; It is wrong to say – a red new dress

blocks.text: (A Guide to Patterns and Usage in English, A.S. Hornby)
Rule 159

There are many '-ed' or '-ing' adjective pairs derived from verbs. To avoid mixing these up, remember that the '-ed' adjectives are used for describing how you feel, and the '-ing' adjectives are used for what it is that makes you feel that way.

items.text: I feel tired. (Working in the garden all day is very tiring.)
I am bored. (This grammar lesson is boring.)
She was disappointed. (Her maths test score was disappointing.)

blocks.text: Rule 160
When there are two or more adjectives that are from the same group, the word 'and' is placed between the two adjectives.

items.text: The house is green and red; The library has old and new books.

blocks.text: Rule 161
When there are three or more adjectives from the same adjective group, we place a comma between each of the coordinate adjectives.

items.text: We live in a big green, white and red house at the end of the street.
My friend lost a red, black and white watch.

blocks.text: Remember that a comma is not placed between an adjective and the noun.
Rule 162
If the adjectives aren't usually used together, separate them with a comma or conjunction.

items.text: I'm looking for a small, good-tempered dog to keep as a pet.
My new dog is small and good-tempered.

blocks.text: Rule 163
If you are using multiple adjectives which are commonly put together, there's no need for a comma between the adjectives.

items.text: Look at that sweet little puppy!

blocks.text: Rule 164
Adjectives of quantity show how much of a thing is meant. Adjectives of quantity (like – some, much, little, enough, all, no, any, great, half, sufficient, whole) are used for uncountable nouns only.

items.text: I ate some rice.
It is wrong to say – I ate a few rice.

blocks.text: Rule 165
Numeral adjectives are used for countable nouns only and they show how many persons or things are meant or in what order a person or thing stands.

items.text: I have taught you a few things.
It is wrong to say – I have taught you little things.

blocks.text: Rule 166
'Later' and 'latest' refer to time; 'latter' and 'last' refer to position.

items.text: I reached at 10 am. But he was later than I expected.
It is wrong to say – I reached at 10 am. But he was latter than expected.

blocks.text: Rule 167
When cardinal and ordinal adjectives are used together, an ordinal adjective precedes the cardinal adjective.

items.text: The first four boys will be given the chance.
It is wrong to say – The four first boys will be given the chance.

blocks.text: Rule 168
'Farther' means more distant or advanced; 'further' means additional.

items.text: He insisted on further improvement.
It is wrong to say – He insisted on farther improvement.

blocks.text: Rule 169
We use 'as + adjective/adverb + as' to make comparisons when the things we are comparing are equal in some way.

items.text: The world's biggest bull is as big as a small elephant.
The weather this summer is as bad as last year. It hasn't stopped raining for weeks.

blocks.text: Rule 170
'Each' is used while speaking of two or more things; 'every' is used only while speaking of more than two.

items.text: Each of the two boys will get a prize.
It is wrong to say – Every of the two boys will get a prize.

blocks.text: Remember that 'each' is singular and so a singular verb should be used with it.
Rule 171
To express quantity or degree, 'some' is used in affirmative sentences; 'any' is used in negative or interrogative sentences.

items.text: Have you bought any mangoes?
It is wrong to say – Have you bought some mangoes?

blocks.text: Rule 172
When two qualities of the same person or thing are compared, the comparative in '-er' is not used; rather we use 'more'.

items.text: He is more wise than brave.
It is wrong to say – He is wiser than brave.

blocks.text: Rule 173

The comparative degree denotes the existence of a higher degree of the quality than the positive. In comparing two things, the comparative degree of an adjective should be used and not the superlative degree of adjective. Remember that 'the' is always used before a comparative degree in this case.

items.text: Which is the better of the two?
It is wrong to say – Which is the best of the two?

blocks.text: Rule 174
When comparison is made by means of a comparative degree, the thing compared should be excluded from the class of things with which it is compared by using 'other' or some such word.

items.text: He is cleverer than any other boy in the class.
It is wrong to say – He is cleverer than any boy in the class.

blocks.text: Rule 175

Adjectives and adverbs in the superlative degree are similar to the comparative degree, but use the -est ending and the word 'most' instead. In addition, the article 'the' must be placed before the adjective or adverb in the sentence.

items.text: Justin is the fastest runner on the track team.
Mr. Kapoor spoke the most highly of Ravi than the other interview candidates.

blocks.text: The superlative degree is used when something is being compared to three or more things. A common mistake with double superlatives is using both the ending -est and the word 'most' in the same sentence. Errors with double superlatives can also be identified in the sentence by reading the sentence out aloud. For example, the prior sentence would be incorrect if it was written as follows: "Justin is the most fastest runner on the track team." It would be best to remove 'most' and keep fastest in the superlative degree.
Rule 176

Double comparatives are phrases commonly used for expressing increasing or decreasing returns. Double comparatives are often employed to underline the importance of doing or not doing a certain activity.

items.text: The more you study, the more you learn.
The more time you take, the better your assignment turns in.
The less money I spend, the less I have to worry about saving.
The easier the test is, the longer students will wait to prepare.
The faster the car is, the more dangerous it is to drive.
The crazier the idea is, the more fun it is to try.

blocks.text: The format of double comparatives is as follows: The (more / less) + (noun / noun phrase) subject + verb + , + the (more / less) + (noun) subject + verb. Remember that with 'more' and 'less' you are not comparing adjectives but rather actions. You can compare adjectives in the same way as:
Rule 177
When comparison is made by means of a superlative, the thing compared should include the class of things with which it is compared.

items.text: He is the strongest of all men.
It is wrong to say – He is the strongest of all other men.

blocks.text: Rule 178
When a superlative degree is followed by a noun, in or any other preposition is used. When no noun follows the superlative degree, 'of' is used.

items.text: It is the most expensive car in the world.
I am the happiest girl under the sun.
She is the most sensible of the Smith girls.
He is the brightest of all the students.

blocks.text: Michael Swan : Practical English Usage
Rule 179
When two persons or things are compared, it is important that the same parts of things should be compared.

items.text: The population of Mumbai is greater than that of Delhi.
It is wrong to say – The population of Mumbai is greater than Delhi.

blocks.text: Rule 180
'As...as' is used for comparing two persons or things. In such a case, an adjective in positive degree is used.

items.text: He is as intelligent as his brother.

blocks.text: Rule 181
You should remember that double comparatives and superlatives should not be used.

items.text: He is the cleverest boy in the class.
It is wrong to say – He is the most cleverest boy in the class.
He is wiser than his brother.
It is wrong to say – He is more wiser than his brother.

blocks.text: Rule 182
We use the superlative to compare somebody / something with the whole group to which he/she/it belongs.

items.text: Rani is the prettiest girl in the class. (Here we make a comparison using the superlative degree.)
Rani is prettier than any other girl in the class. (Here we make a comparison using the comparative degree.)
No other girl in the class is so (as) pretty as Rani. (Here we make a comparison using the positive degree.)
Tea is the most popular beverage in the world.
Tea is more popular than any other beverage.
No other beverage is so (as) popular as tea.

blocks.text: Rule 183
The comparative adjectives, like superior, inferior, senior, junior, prior, anterior, posterior, prefer, etc. should be followed by 'to' instead of 'than'.

items.text: He is senior to me.
It is wrong to say – He is senior than me.

blocks.text: Rule 184
Adjectives, like unique, ideal, perfect, complete, entire, extreme, chief, full, square and round, which do not admit different degrees of comparison should not be compared.

items.text: It is a unique thing.
It is wrong to say – It is the most unique thing.

blocks.text: Rule 185
All the adjectives which refer to the same noun should be in the same degree of comparison.

items.text: He is the wisest and most honest worker in the office.
It is wrong to say – He is the wisest and honest worker in the office.

blocks.text: Rule 186
'Elder' and 'eldest' should be used for persons only. To be precise, they should be used for the members of the same family only. 'Older' and 'oldest' are used for both persons and things.

items.text: He is my elder brother.
It is wrong to say – He is my older brother.

blocks.text: Rule 187

You can use articles before adjectives which are followed by the nouns in which they modify. If there is no associated noun, then they can't be used. Do not attach articles to adjectives in declarative statements which use adjectives following the nouns, like: the car – the fast car; a dog – a happy dog.

items.text: She is a young girl.
This is a nice shirt. — Here, the adjectives 'young' and 'nice' appear before the nouns as descriptive elements rather than part of declarative statements. So, the article is needed.

blocks.text: Rule 188

You can tell whether a word is an adverb or not by considering its function in the sentence. If it is describing one of the three parts of speech, i.e. a verb, an adjective or other adverb, you can simply say that it is an adverb.
Rule 189
Adverbs describe verbs (actions). They give more detail about the action.

items.text: My cat eats slowly. — In the sentence above, 'slowly' is an adverb since it describes the way my cat eats.

blocks.text: How does my cat eat? Slowly. Therefore, we can say that adverbs generally answer the question 'How'.
Rule 190
Adverbs are usually placed after the verbs.

items.text: He speaks clearly.

blocks.text: Rule 191
Adverbs can also modify adjectives and other adverbs.

items.text: The woman is quite pretty.
This book is more interesting than the last one.
The weather report is almost always right. — In the last sentence, the adverb 'almost' is modifying the adverb 'always', and they're both modifying 'right'.

blocks.text: Rule 192
Adverbs are normally formed by adding '-ly' at the end of adjectives, like: quick – quickly For adjectives that end in '-l' or '-e', we simply add '-ly'.

items.text: special + ly = specially; nice + ly = nicely; polite + ly = politely

blocks.text: However, there are some exceptions. true = truly; whole = wholly; due = duly; full = fully
Rule 193
First in itself is an adverb. So, adding –ly to it is wrong. We should write – first, secondly, thirdly, etc.
Rule 194
When there is an object, the adverb is usually placed after the verb + object.

items.text: I put the vase carefully on the table.
I read the book quickly.
Quickly, I changed my opinion.

blocks.text: But you should always remember that adverbs are never positioned between the verb and the object. However, it is wrong to say – I read quickly the book. Sometimes, adverbs are placed at the beginning of a clause.
Rule 195
When a verb is used before its subject, it is called inversion. Inversion is of two types : Partial Inversion, Complete Inversion

items.text: Hardly does he meet her.
Here comes the President.
Just outside the gate was standing a beggar.

blocks.text: The first example illustrates Partial Inversion; the last two illustrate Complete Inversion.
Rule 196
'Late' is both an adverb and an adjective; it means the opposite of early. 'Lately' is also an adverb; it means 'recently'. 'Late' as an adverb means 'not on time'.

items.text: Well, I couldn't find my classroom, so I got to the classroom a bit late and then I had to sing a song in front of the other students!
The programme started late.
We had a late breakfast.

blocks.text: Again, 'late' as an adjective means 'after the usual time'.
Rule 197
The adverb too is used for showing undesirable extremes. It has a negative meaning.

items.text: She is too fat.
He is too tired.

blocks.text: Rule 198
An infinitive structure is often used after too + adjective /adverb/ determiner.

items.text: He is too tired to work.
It is too hot to go outside.
We arrived too late to have dinner.
It is too late for us to begin a new lesson.
It happened a bit too soon.
She appeared a little too confident.

blocks.text: Sometimes the infinitive may have its own subject. In such cases, it is usually introduced by 'for'. Expressions used for modifying comparative adjectives can also be used for modifying 'too'.
Rule 199
Some adverbs, like – very, extremely, really, totally, absolutely, quite, fairly, well are used for modifying adjectives. These adverbs are normally placed before adjectives.

items.text: It was very hot yesterday.
He is totally crazy.

blocks.text: Rule 200

There are some adverbs which are used for describing how frequently we do an activity. These are called adverbs of frequency. Adverbs of frequency include – always, usually, normally / generally, often / frequently, sometimes, occasionally, seldom, hardly ever / rarely, never.
Rule 201
An adverb of frequency goes before a main verb (except with 'to be'.) Subject + adverb + main verb

items.text: I always remember to do my homework.
He normally gets good marks in exams.

blocks.text: Rule 202
An adverb of frequency goes after the verb 'to be'. Subject + to be + adverb

items.text: They are never pleased to see me.
She isn't usually bad-tempered.

blocks.text: Rule 203

When we use an auxiliary verb (have, will, must, might, could, would, can, etc.), the adverb is placed between the auxiliary and the main verb. This is also true for 'to be'. Subject + auxiliary + adverb + main verb

items.text: He can sometimes beat me in a race.
They might never see each other again.

blocks.text: Rule 204
There are some adverbs, like – usually, normally, often, frequently, sometimes, occasionally which we can use at the beginning of a sentence.

items.text: Normally it rains on a humid day.
Occasionally, I like to eat Chinese food.

blocks.text: But, there are some adverbs which we cannot use at the beginning of a sentence; they include always, seldom, rarely, hardly, ever, never.
Rule 205
We use hardly ever and never with only positive, and not with negative verbs.

items.text: She hardly ever comes to my parties.
They never say 'thank you'.

blocks.text: Rule 206
We use ever in questions and negative statements.

items.text: Have you ever been to Australia?
I haven't ever been to Switzerland.

blocks.text: Rule 207
For adjectives that end in '-y', we remove the '-y' and add '-ily' to make adverbs.

items.text: crazy = crazily; happy = happily

blocks.text: Rule 208
For adjectives that end in '–le' we remove the '-e' and add '-y' to make adverbs.

items.text: idle = idly; noble = nobly; horrible = horribly; terrible = terribly

blocks.text: Rule 209
If an adjective ends in '-ic', we add '-ally' to make an adverb.

items.text: ironic = ironically; realistic = realistically;
enthusiastic = enthusiastically

blocks.text: But, there is an exception. Like: public – publicly
Rule 210
There are adverbs which are irregular. They do not form by adding '-ly' at the end. Moreover, their form remains the same in both an adjective and an adverb.

items.text: fast (adjective) = fast (adverb) – The man drives very fast (quickly).
hard (adjective) = hard (adverb) – His decision is very hard. (strong)

blocks.text: Rule 211
Adverbs of manner tell us how something is done. An adverb of manner is usually placed at the end of a sentence or before the main verb.

items.text: Tom drives quickly.
She slowly opened the door.
Mary waited for him patiently.

blocks.text: Rule 212
An adverb of manner cannot be put between a verb and its direct object. It must be placed either before the verb or at the end of the clause.

items.text: He ate the chocolate cake greedily. Or He greedily ate the chocolate cake.
It is wrong to say – He ate greedily the chocolate cake.
He gave us the money generously. Or He generously gave us the money.
It is wrong to say – He gave us generously the money.

blocks.text: Rule 213
If there is a preposition before the object of the verb, you can place the adverb of manner either before the preposition or after the object.

items.text: The child ran happily towards his mother.
The child ran towards his mother happily.

blocks.text: Rule 214
Adverbs of manner should always come immediately after verbs which have no object (intransitive verbs).

items.text: The town grew quickly after 1995.
He waited patiently for his mother to arrive.

blocks.text: Rule 215

The position of the adverb is important when there is more than one verb in a sentence. If the adverb is placed before or after the main verb, it modifies only that verb. If the adverb is placed after a clause, then it modifies the whole action described by the clause.

items.text: She quickly agreed to re-type the letter.
He quietly asked me to leave the house.

blocks.text: Rule 216
Sometimes an adverb of manner is placed before a verb + object to add emphasis.

items.text: She gently woke the sleeping woman up.
He angrily slammed the door.

blocks.text: Rule 217
Many frequency words are adverbs as well – very, much, more and many can be adverbs.

items.text: The very pretty girl was in the car.
The much smarter boy won the race.

blocks.text: Rule 218
It is often mistaken when you use an adjective in place of an adverb, and vice versa.

items.text: He behaved very bad on the field trip. — The sentence in the example above is incorrect, because bad is modifying or describing 'behaved', which is a verb. It should be – He behaved very badly.

blocks.text: On the other hand, if you say – His behaviour is bad – would be correct, because in this case, the word bad is an adjective describing the noun 'behaviour'.
Rule 219
It is often confusing to use adverbs and adjectives with the words 'good' and 'well'.
Remember – 'good' is an adjective that should modify nouns (the good boy); while 'well' is an adverb that modifies a verb (he listens well), or even an adjective (the well educated boy).
Rule 220
Adverbs of time tell us when / at what time something is done. An adverb of time is usually placed at the end of a sentence. It can also be used at the beginning of a sentence followed by a comma.

items.text: The meeting is next week.
Yesterday, we decided to take a walk.
I've already bought my tickets to the concert.

blocks.text: Some of the most common adverbs of time are: yet, already, yesterday, tomorrow, next week / month / year, last week / month / year, now, ago. These are used with other time expressions, such as days of the week.
Rule 221
Adverbs of place tell us where something is done. An adverb of place is usually placed at the end of a sentence, but it can also follow the verb.

items.text: I decided to rest over there.
She'll wait for you in the room downstairs.
Peter walked above me upstairs.

blocks.text: Rule 222

Adverbs of frequency tell us how often something is repeatedly done. These adverbs include: usually, sometimes, never, often, rarely, etc. You can put an adverb of frequency directly before the main verb.

items.text: She rarely goes to parties.
I often read a newspaper.
He usually gets up at six o'clock.

blocks.text: Rule 223
Sometimes, an adverb of frequency is placed at the beginning of a sentence. The most common of them are : sometimes and often.

items.text: Sometimes, I enjoy staying at home instead of going on vacation.
Often, Peter will telephone his mother before he leaves for work.

blocks.text: Rule 224
Adverbs can also modify adjectives. In this case, the adverb is placed before the adjective.

items.text: She is extremely happy; They are absolutely sure.

blocks.text: Rule 225
Never use 'very' with an adjective that expresses an increased quality of a basic adjective, like – fantastic.

items.text: She is an absolutely fantastic piano player.
It will be wrong to say – She is an absolutely very fantastic piano player.

blocks.text: Rule 226
Some adjectives change their form when they become adverbs.

items.text: good (adjective) = well (adverb) – You speak English very well.

blocks.text: Rule 227
Many words, although they end in '-ly', are not adverbs.

items.text: a lonely girl; an elderly person

blocks.text: Rule 228
Adverbs of degree tell us about the intensity or degree of an action, an adjective or another adverb.

items.text: The water was extremely cold.
He was just leaving; She has almost finished.

blocks.text: Some common adverbs of degree are: almost, nearly, quite, just, too, enough, hardly, scarcely, completely, very, extremely. An adverb of degree is usually placed – (i) before the adjective or adverb they are modifying (ii) before the main verb
Rule 229
The use of 'at present' and 'presently' is different and should not be confused. 'At present' means 'at the present time' and 'presently' means 'shortly'.

items.text: Nothing more can be done at present. — It is wrong to say – Nothing more can be done presently.
He will come back presently. — It is wrong to say – He will come back at present.

blocks.text: Rule 230

The use of 'hard' and 'hardly' is quite different. 'Hard' means 'diligently', 'strenuously'; while 'hardly' means 'scarcely' or 'not at all'. These two adverbial forms of 'hard' must be remembered and should not be confused.

items.text: He tried hard to win the race. — It is wrong to say – He tried hardly to win the race.
She has eaten hardly anything today. — It is wrong to say – She has eaten hard anything today.

blocks.text: Rule 231
Remember that 'hardly' is an adverb which means rarely; whereas 'hard' is an adjective which means tough; rigid. Their usage is totally different.

items.text: It is a hard job.
It is wrong to say – It is a hardly job.

blocks.text: Rule 232
In a sentence which is based on 'too .... to' format, we cannot replace 'to' with 'cannot'. If we replace 'to' with 'cannot', 'too' also must be replaced by 'so that'.

items.text: He is too weak to walk.
He is so weak that he cannot walk.

blocks.text: But it will be wrong if we say – He is too weak so that he cannot walk.
Rule 233
'Too' means 'more than required' and it is used with an Unpleasant Adjective. So we cannot use 'too glad', 'too happy', 'too pleasant', 'too healthy', etc.

items.text: I am very glad to meet you. — It is wrong to say – I am too glad to meet you.

blocks.text: Rule 234
'Much too' is followed by an Unpleasant Adjective (Much too + Unpleasant Adjective), whereas 'too much' is followed by a noun (Too much + Noun).

items.text: His failure is much too painful for me. — It is wrong to say – His failure is too much painful for me.
His wife's rude behaviour gives him too much pain. — It is wrong to say – His wife's rude behaviour gives him much too pain.

blocks.text: Rule 235
The use of two negatives in a sentence is not allowed. Two negatives cancel each other. Hence, two negatives should not be used in the same sentence unless we make an affirmation.

items.text: I have not got any; It is wrong to say – I have not got none.

blocks.text: Rule 236
'Quite' and 'all' are not used together.

items.text: He is quite right — or, He is all right. — But it is wrong to say – He is quite all right.

blocks.text: Though Oxford Advanced Learner's Dictionary asserts that it is a correct sentence.
Rule 237
A/An + Fairly + Adjective + Noun — or, Rather + A + Adjective But we cannot use a Pleasant Adjective with 'rather' and an Unpleasant Adjective with 'fairly'.

items.text: a fairly good book
rather a difficult problem
It was a fairly good book. — It is wrong to say – It was a rather good book.

blocks.text: Rule 238
'Enough' when used as an Adverb is preceded by a positive degree of an adjective or adverb.

items.text: He is great enough to pardon you. — It is wrong to say – He is greater enough to pardon you.

blocks.text: Rule 239
'Enough' goes after the adjective or adverb that it is modifying, and not before it as other adverbs do. It can be used both in positive and negative sentences.

items.text: Is your coffee hot enough? ; This box isn't big enough.
He didn't work hard enough.

blocks.text: Rule 240
'Enough' is often followed by 'to' + infinitive.

items.text: He didn't work hard enough to pass the exam.
Is your coffee hot enough to drink?
She's not old enough to get married.

blocks.text: Rule 241
'Enough' can also be followed by 'for someone' or 'for something'.

items.text: The dress was big enough for me.
She's not experienced enough for this job.
He didn't work hard enough for a promotion.

blocks.text: Rule 242
'Enough' as a determiner meaning 'as much/many as necessary' goes before the noun it modifies. It is used with a countable noun in the plural and with an uncountable noun.

items.text: We have enough bread.
They don't have enough food.
We have enough pens.

blocks.text: Rule 243
To modify a verb, an adjective or another adverb, we use an adverb.

items.text: She writes very carefully. — It is wrong to say – She writes very careful. 'Careful' is an adjective which cannot modify the adverb 'very'. Therefore, 'carefully' (adverb) must be used in place of adjective 'careful'.

blocks.text: Rule 244
'Much' is used before a past participle and an adjective or adverb of a comparative degree; and 'very' is used before the present participle, and an adjective and an adverb of a positive degree.

items.text: The news is very surprising. — It is wrong to say – The news is much surprising.
I was much surprised at hearing the news. — It is wrong to say – I was very surprised at hearing the news.

blocks.text: Rule 245
'Much' is used with an uncountable noun and 'more' with a countable noun. There is no connection between much and more with the comparative and superlative.

items.text: I have much interest in cooking.
I have more friends to help me in problems.

blocks.text: Rule 246

Adjectives with two syllables can form the comparative either by adding -er or by preceding the adjective with 'more'. These adjectives form the superlative either by adding -est or by preceding the adjective with 'most'. In many cases, both forms are used, although one usage will be more common than the other. If you are not sure whether a two-syllable adjective can take a comparative or superlative ending, use 'more' and 'most' instead. For adjectives ending in y, change the y to an i before adding the ending.

items.text: Adjective — Comparative — Superlative
tilted — more tilted — most tilted
tangled — more tangled — most tangled
Adjective — Comparative — Superlative
important — more important — most important
expansive — more expansive — most expansive
adequate — more adequate — most adequate

blocks.text: Adjectives with three or more syllables form the comparative by putting 'more' in front of the adjective, and the superlative by putting 'most' in front.
Rule 247
'Too' is always an adverb, but it has two distinct meanings, each with its own usage patterns. Too as an adverb meaning 'also' goes at the end of the phrase it modifies.

items.text: I would like to go swimming too, if you will let me come.
Is this gift for me too?

blocks.text: Rule 248
Too as an adverb meaning 'excessively' goes before the adjective or adverb it modifies. It can be used in both affirmative and negative sentences.

items.text: He works too hard; Isn't she too young?

blocks.text: Rule 249
Too is often followed by 'to' + the infinitive.

items.text: The coffee was too hot to drink.
I am not too tired to go out tonight.
Don't you work too hard to have any free time?

blocks.text: Rule 250
'Too' can also be followed by 'for someone' or 'for something'.

items.text: The coffee was too hot for me.
The dress was too small for her.
He's not too old for this job.

blocks.text: Rule 251
'Ago' is always used with Past Indefinite tense. Therefore, if 'ago' is used in a sentence, that sentence must be in the Past Indefinite tense.

items.text: He came a month ago. — It is wrong to say – He has come a month ago.

blocks.text: Rule 252
'At present' means 'at this moment' and it is used with Present tense; whereas 'presently' and 'shortly' are used for referring to future action and generally used with Future Indefinite tense.

items.text: At present he is in the room. — It is wrong to say – Presently he is in the room.

blocks.text: Rule 253
'Early' means 'just after the beginning of anything' and 'soon' means 'just after a point of time'.

items.text: Roses blossomed early this spring.
The firing at the Line of Control started soon after midnight.

blocks.text: Rule 254
The sentence which starts with 'seldom', 'never', 'hardly', 'rarely' or 'scarcely' takes an inverse structure, i.e. Verb + Subject structure.

items.text: Seldom had I seen such a beautiful sight. — It is wrong to say – Seldom I had seen such a beautiful sight.

blocks.text: Rule 255
Inversion is also used in a sentence which starts with here / there / away / out / up / indoor or outdoor and main verb, or Aux. + Main Verb is used before the subject.

items.text: Away went Sita. — It is wrong to say – Away Sita went.

blocks.text: Rule 256
'A few' (for a countable noun) and 'a little' (for an uncountable noun) describe the quantity in a positive way, implying that although the speaker may not have much, he has enough.

items.text: I've got a few friends. = I have enough friends.
I have a few flowers in my garden. = I have enough flowers.
I've got a little money. = I have enough money.
I have a little free time on Thursdays. = I have enough free time.
Few people visited him in hospital. = He had almost no visitors, or perhaps no visitors at all.
I've seen few birds around here. = There are almost no birds, or perhaps not a single bird.
He had little money for treats. = Almost no money, or perhaps no money at all.
I have little time for TV = Almost no time, or perhaps no time at all.

blocks.text: 'Few' (for a countable noun) and 'little' (for an uncountable noun) describe the quantity in a negative way. They may actually indicate a total lack of the noun, but are more polite than saying so directly.
Rule 257
A preposition must always be followed by a noun or pronoun. That noun is called the object of the preposition. A verb can't be the object of a preposition.

items.text: The bone was for the dog. (Here, the preposition for is followed by the noun 'dog').
But, if we say – The bone was for walked. – This is not correct. The preposition for is followed by a verb 'walked', which can't be the object of a preposition.

blocks.text: Rule 258
As a preposition must always be followed by a noun and should have an object, it usually shouldn't be used at the end of a sentence.

items.text: The table is where I put my books on. — It is a wrong usage. Here, the use of the preposition 'on' isn't necessary. We could take the 'on' out of the sentence and the meaning would be the same.

But, if you say – 'I turned the TV on.' — It is correct. Here, if you remove the 'on' from the end of the sentence, it would change the meaning. Instead of switching on the set, you would be saying that you turned the TV itself.

blocks.text: Rule 259
Preposition 'to' is used for showing the person or thing that receives something.

items.text: He gave it to his sister
Who did she address the letter to ?
I am deeply grateful to my parents.

blocks.text: Rule 260
Prepositions like – at, on and in have dual roles, telling both time and place.

items.text: The class is at 8 o'clock. (time)
Meet me at the school. (place)
The election is on Thursday. (time)
Is your name on the ballot? (place)
Spring officially begins in three days. (time)
We're still up to our knees in snow. (place)

blocks.text: Rule 261
Prepositions of direction, like – to, on, onto, in, and into tell you where to go or where to put something.

items.text: It's time to go to the class.
Put on your gloves and shoes.
Make sure your books are in your shelf.

blocks.text: Rule 262

Prepositions 'during' and 'while' are used for referring to something in action. 'During' is a preposition which is used before a noun (during + noun) for saying when something happens. It does not tell us how long it happened.

items.text: Nobody spoke during the presentation.
We get plenty of snow here during winter.
The phone rang while I was watching TV.
I met him while we were studying in the library.

blocks.text: 'While' is used for talking about two things that are happening at the same time. The length of time is not important. Remember : 'while' is used with a subject and a verb (while + subject + verb).
Rule 263
Prepositions – 'onto' and 'into' are used with verbs that imply some sort of movement or progress.

items.text: The plane landed onto the runway. — 'To land' is not a verb which necessarily requires movement; it's referring to the moment when the plane actually stops on the runway. We can say – The plane landed on the runway.
But – The plane glided onto the runway. — 'Gliding' most certainly implies motion, so we can use onto with it.
The caterpillar changed into a butterfly.
The caterpillar changed in a butterfly.
Put the book in the box.
Put the book into the box.

blocks.text: Remember that – 'into' can usually be replaced by in.
Rule 264
Nouns and prepositions often work together in common phrases, like – on vacation, by chance, on purpose, by accident, difference between, on strike, a solution to.

items.text: Can we find a solution to this problem?
There is currently a great demand for organic products.
It's the season for celebration.
What's the cause of this accident?

blocks.text: Rule 265
Adjectives and prepositions are commonly used in phrases. The adjective usually goes before the preposition.

items.text: I'm really excited about this project.
He was found guilty of fraud and tax evasion.
Students often get worried about writing exams.
The world felt sorry for the victims of the tsunami.

blocks.text: Rule 266
Verbs and prepositions are also used in common phrases. The verb generally goes in front of the preposition.

items.text: Do you agree to the new guidelines?
You get what you pay for.
This novel gave me a lot to think about.

blocks.text: Rule 267
The verb and the preposition may be separated, especially if the sentence is formally written so the preposition isn't at the end.

items.text: Didn't I warn you about leaving things until the last minute?
To whom does this book belong? (Who does this book belong to?)
Could you please explain this maths problem to me?

blocks.text: Some other examples of verb/preposition combinations are ask for, depend on, look after, wait for, rely on, dream on, lead on, do something for someone, be careful of, be careful with, be disappointed by, boast about, complain about, in conclusion, and search for.
Rule 268

It's a common rule which states that you should never end a sentence with a preposition. In conversation and informal writing, ending a sentence with a preposition is perfectly acceptable. It's only in formal writing that we still follow the rule.

items.text: Which box should this go into? (Into which box should this go?)
Come in. (Come into the house.)
When I glanced at the table, I saw the dog was hiding beneath. (When I glanced at the table, I saw the dog was hiding beneath it.)

blocks.text: Rule 269
Objective case (of noun or pronoun) is used after a preposition.

items.text: I do not depend on him. — It is wrong to say – I do not depend on he.

blocks.text: Rule 270
A preposition generally, but not always, goes before its noun or pronoun.

items.text: That is something I cannot agree to.
How many of you can I depend on?
But, if you say – Where did you get this at? Where did he go to? — These sentences are wrong. The correct form of these sentences will be – Where did you get this? Where did he go?

blocks.text: The prepositions 'at' and 'to' at the end of these sentences are meaningless and wrong to use.
Rule 271

'Due to' and 'owing to' are similar in meaning to 'on account of' and 'because of'. They are all prepositions used with noun phrases and are often used interchangeably. They indicate that something happened as a result of something or introduce the reason for something happening. Remember, verb add is followed by preposition 'to'.

items.text: He was kept in after school due to/owing to his bad behaviour. = He was kept in after school on account of/because of his bad behaviour.
Due to/owing to a broken propeller, the new cruise liner returned immediately to the port. = The new cruise liner returned immediately to the port because of/on account of a broken propeller.

blocks.text: Rule 272
The preposition 'like' means 'similar to' or 'similarly to'. It should be followed by an object of the preposition (noun, pronoun, noun phrase), not by a subject and verb.

items.text: You look like your mother. — That is, you look similar to her. (Mother is the object of the preposition 'like'.)
But it will be wrong if you say – You look like your mother does. (Avoid 'like' with noun + verb.)
